_comment: Every number the History Writer's deterministic tools use. Content, so it is tuned by PR with no rebuild and no prompt change. The tier requirements and sourceRatio are INITIAL calibrations from the Seattle Landmarks corpus, not measurements of long-form stories: the first pilot story measures the real ratio on the chapters the author accepts without edits, and these move to that. Read by tools/_hw.py.
_fetchMinIntervalSeconds: fetch.py waits at least this long between two requests to the SAME host, across every process on the Mac, so parallel scouts do not get an archive to rate-limit them.
_fetchHostIntervals: Stricter spacing for hosts that rate-limit. www.loc.gov (the Chronicling America search) blocked the scouts for over an hour after about ten searches in a burst (2026-10-02); tile.loc.gov, which serves the page text, did not. A host may also be LOOSER than the default: the Wikipedia and Wikimedia APIs serve one request at a time quickly and ask clients only to stay serial, which fame.py does (ranking a thousand names at 1.5 s apart would take 25 minutes).
_minQuoteWords: Evidence for a claim is a verbatim, contiguous quote of at least this many words from the claimed source's fetched text. Same floor as the landmark writer.
_eventEvidenceRequired: A dossier event's `evidence` (a verbatim quote of at least minQuoteWords words from one of its sources) is always checked when present, and an event whose quote fails never counts. When true, an event with NO evidence does not count either, so no tier rests on a model's word. False only so the ten Black Seattle dossiers scouted before events carried evidence (2026-10-02) keep their tiers while the pilot runs; turn it on before the next scout, and before scouts run on a cheaper model (design D8).
_verbatimCopyWindowWords: Prose may not reproduce this many consecutive words from a facts-only (copyrighted, non-commercial or no-derivatives) source outside quotation marks. Quotations of a person's own words are checked against the claims instead.
_eraShareMax: Era context (sourced claims about the time and place, kind 'era') may be at most this share of a chapter's words, so the person stays the subject.
_eraSentencesMax: voice.md §9 (2026-10-28, Lawrence: 'just drop a few factual nuggets here and there'): a chapter with more sentences of era context than this gets a note (era_nuggets, soft) from tools/era.py. A note, not a limit: era_share stays the hard cap. A domain sets null to measure era context its own way. The 20 Black Seattle stories as published: 17 of 112 chapters over 4.
_eraRepeat: tools/era.py: an era claim repeats one another story of the series already tells (era_repeat, soft) when both quote a run of runWords words from the same source, or their sentences share `names` names and years (not counting those in more than a quarter of the series' era sentences, such as the city) and `overlap` of their content words. Measured 2026-10-28 on the published Black Seattle book: 18 repeats, the 1889 fire and the Pioneer Square settlement among them; a looser match (any 4 content words) also paired two different cable-car lines.
_thinChapterWords: richness.py plan notes a chapter whose aim falls under this many words: merge it with a neighbour. Each chapter costs a writer and an auditor whatever its length (the tier-B stories, 2026-10-05).
_sourceRatio: A story's ceiling is at most this many words per word of source text about the subject. A guess calibrated on landmark entries; the pilot replaces it.
_starved: No minimum length — but a chapter allotted at least starvedMinEvents dated events that comes in under starvedFraction of its ceiling has abandoned a rich allotment (the v6 lesson: brevity is not a virtue in itself).
_encyclopediaPublishers: Tier A requires sources beyond these, because a story built only from summaries of other work has nothing new to say.
_mode: biography: sourced events across at least biographyMinLifeStages life stages. episode: otherwise, when at least episodeWindowShare of dated events fall inside one episodeWindowYears window. ensemble: otherwise — the person is told through the community the record does hold.
_tiers: Checked A, then B, then C; the first whose every requirement is met wins. Below C the person goes on a research list, not into a story.
_tiersWordsAboutSubject: wordsAboutSubject floors are each tier's minimum length divided by sourceRatio (10000/0.6, 4000/0.6, 1500/0.6, rounded up), so a tier's ceiling can never fall below its own minimum. Change them together.
_introWords: voice.md §13: the introduction's length. Over the ceiling fails; under the floor is a note. A first measure, set when the author asked for introductions on the first pilot (2026-10-03).
_editor: tools/editor.py, the book editor (2026-10-04). check: a run of repeatRunWords words, repeatContentWords of them not stopwords, shared by sentences in two chapters is told twice; sentences whose content words overlap by similarSentence or more and whose numbers conflict disagree; a body chapter balanceRatio times the middle one, or 1/balanceRatio, is out of scale; a chapter whose average sentence is sentenceDrift off the book's drifts. verify: at most maxNotes notes are read, and at most maxSuggestionsPerChapter suggestions a chapter reach the author.
_targetOverrun: voice_lint: a chapter more than this many times its share of plan.targetWords gets a soft over_target note (2026-10-04: the third story's writers wrote 5,228 words against a 3,500-word target they never saw).

topics.daily life: a home, a meal, a day's work, what things cost, clothes, light after dark
topics.health: how long people lived, sickness, wounds, childbirth, what a doctor could and could not do
topics.technology: tools, building, machines, materials, and what each side had that the other did not
topics.travel: roads, rivers, ships, how far a day took you, how fast news moved
topics.customs: belief, law, family, rank, feasts and burials: what would strike us as strange
topics.peoples: who a people were, what they called themselves, their language, and what became of them
topics.warfare: arms and armour, pay and food, how an army lived between battles
topics.money and trade: coins, markets, what was bought and sold, and with whom
topics.news and records: how people learned the news, who could read, what was written down and why
topics.forces of the time: the migrations, markets and laws of the period that shaped where a life could go

world._topics: world.py check refuses a fact whose `topic` is not one of these. A domain may replace the list. The author, 2026-10-28, on the Black Seattle lives ("why there were so many newspapers at that time", "what were the forces of Black migration") and on Caesar in Gaul ("living conditions", "average life span", "what happened if you got sick or injured", "what kind of technology", "cultural customs", "Who were the Gauls? Were they proto-French?").

_context: voice.md §9, the world around the story: a body chapter whose ceiling reaches minChapterWords picks world facts, about one per wordsPerPick words, within perChapter; each told in at most maxWordsPerPick words (a sentence or two, a short paragraph at most). Only for a story whose project.json names a `world` pool. The author, 2026-10-28: "a few sentences or a paragraph here and there every page or two or three might help pull the reader into the time", "not to the point where it's distracting".
